sentences.text: Foraminacephale was a small, two-legged plant-eater defined by a thickened skull cap.
Gregory S. Paul estimated this animal measured 1.5 meters in length and weighed 10 kilograms.
The genus name combines the Latin word foramina, meaning holes, with cephale, the Greek-derived form for head, referring to the multiple perforations covering the top of the dome.
The top surface of the skull dome features many small pits known as foramina.
A tall, mostly smooth bar of the squamosal bone sits underneath the dome, featuring six nodes along the bottom edge and one additional corner node.
This species is distinguished by prominent grooves between the central and lateral lobes of the dome and a slit-like opening of the temporal bone.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of Foraminacephale at 1.5 meters and its weight at 10 kilograms in 2016.
Histological analysis showed that Foraminacephale domes became less porous with age, ranging from 1.67% empty space in juveniles to 0.25% in adults.
The holotype of Foraminacephale is specimen CMN 1423, a nearly complete skull dome collected in Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, in 1902.
The fossil layers containing Foraminacephale belong to the Dinosaur Park Formation of the Belly River Group.
Lawrence Lambe first assigned the holotype specimen to a new species of Stegoceras in 1918.
The specimen was later reassigned to the genus Prenocephale in 2000 and then to Sphaerotholus in 2010.
The holotype specimen CMN 1423 is an almost complete frontoparietal dome collected from the Provincial Dinosaur Park in Alberta, Canada.
Various other fragments representing juveniles, subadults, and adults have been found in that geological formation.
A specimen from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation previously assigned to Foraminacephale, CMN 11316, was reidentified as an indeterminate juvenile pachycephalosaur.
Micro-CT scans of a potential Foraminacephale specimen support the hypothesis that pachycephalosaurids likely engaged in head-butting behavior.
Histological analysis showed that Foraminacephale domes became less porous with age, ranging from 1.67% empty space in juveniles to 0.25% in adults.
The supratemporal fenestrae in Foraminacephale are slit-like and seal shut very early in development, unlike the round openings that remain open longer in Stegoceras.
Measurements of 27 different points on 21 Foraminacephale skulls showed that the dome became proportionally taller with age but did not widen significantly.
Histology showed that domes became less porous with age; the smallest specimen's skull had 1.67% empty space, while the largest had 0.25%.
Generally, the frontal zone of the dome was more porous than the parietal zone.
Unlike young Stegoceras which have a flat dome, even the smallest Foraminacephale specimens have a slightly domed parietal.

The supratemporal fenestrae in Foraminacephale skulls are slit-shaped, unlike the rounded ones in Stegoceras, and sealed earlier in ontogenetic development rather than remaining visible throughout life.
In Foraminacephale, the squamosal and postorbital bones became part of the dome much faster, the dome thickened at a slower rate, and the sides were less angular than in Stegoceras.
A 2016 phylogenetic analysis placed Foraminacephale within the Pachycephalosaurinae, more derived than Stegoceras but more basal than Prenocephale.
A 2016 phylogenetic analysis found Foraminacephale to be a member of the subfamily Pachycephalosaurinae, in a position more derived than Stegoceras but more basal than Prenocephale.
The parent group of Foraminacephale is Pachycephalosaurinae.
Foraminacephale belongs to the family Pachycephalosauridae.
Foraminacephale is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Foraminacephale was a pachycephalosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Campanian stage in Canada.
Foraminacephale lived approximately 77 to 73 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
Foraminacephale lived during the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

Due to a lack of understanding of pachycephalosaur growth, researchers have debated whether material from the Belly River Group represents a single species or four different genera.

The 2016 description of Foraminacephale recognized four different pachycephalosaur taxa from the Belly River Group: Stegoceras, Foraminacephale, Hanssuesia, and Colepiocephale, though specimens referred to Hanssuesia likely represent more than one known species.
